title: Right now, not usually — and getting around town
title_target: आप कहाँ जा रही हैं? — aap kahaaⁿ jaa rahii haiⁿ?
goal: Say what is happening right now, and get around in India — including the sentence you need when the meter is "broken".

dialogs.title: संवाद — An auto to the station
dialogs.intro: Ani runs into Rahul in the street. This conversation introduces the "-ing" form you will use every day — and, in line ten, a sentence you will hear so often you'll know it by heart without trying.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Hey Ani! Where are you going?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: I'm going to the market. And you?
lines.literal: I — market — go — -ing(fem.) — am. and — you?

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: I'm going to the station. A friend of mine is on his way.
lines.literal: I — station — go — -ing(masc.) — am. friend — come — -ing(masc.) — is.

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: No, by auto. It's really hot.
lines.literal: no, auto — by. very — heat — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: I'm taking an auto too. Shall we go together?
lines.literal: I — also — auto — take — -ing(fem.) — am. together — shall-we-go?

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: Two hundred? Use the meter, bhaiya.
lines.literal: two — hundred? meter — by — please-go — brother.

lines.speaker: ऑटो वाला:
lines.id: The meter's broken, sir. A hundred, okay?
lines.literal: meter — broken — is — sir. hundred — in — will-go?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: (slowly — with) question — this — always — like-this — happens — is?

lines.speaker: राहुल:
lines.id: (laughing) Yes, always. That's Delhi for you.
lines.literal: (laughing — while) yes, always. this-very — after-all — Delhi — is.

notes: **The "-ing" form = stem + रहा/रही/रहे + होना.** Three words, and each has a job. **रहा · रही · रहे** follow the gender and number of the subject, just like -ता/-ती/-ते in Unit 4. **होना** (हूँ/है/हैं/हो) shows who the subject is. The part in front — the verb stem — never changes at all.

**⚠️ This is the difference beginners most often ignore.** *मैं खाती हूँ* = "I eat (habitually)". *मैं खा रही हूँ* = "I am eating". English makes this split too ("I eat" vs "I'm eating"), so trust that instinct — Hindi is even stricter about it, and using the habitual form for something happening now sounds truly odd. If it's happening right now, use रहा है — no exceptions.
**Quick test: could you add "right now"?** "I'm going to the market (right now)" → **जा रही हूँ**. "I (usually) go to the market on Saturdays" → **जाती हूँ**. The test works nine times out of ten.

**The "-ing" form also covers near-future plans**, just like English. *मैं कल दिल्ली जा रही हूँ* means "I'm going to Delhi tomorrow" — not gone yet, but settled. This isn't an exception; the form simply covers both "in progress" and "already scheduled".

**Vehicles take से, but walking doesn't.** *बस **से***, *ट्रेन **से***, *ऑटो **से***, *मेट्रो **से*** — but **पैदल** stands alone, with nothing after it. ⚠️ Don't say *पैदल से*; that mistake is heard instantly.

**चलना is not जाना, and the difference is useful.** **जाना** = to go somewhere. **चलना** = to walk, move, set off together. That's why "let's go" is **चलिए** or **चलें**, not *जाइए* — which sounds more like "go away". ⚠️ *चलो!* to a friend means "come on, let's go!", while *जाओ!* means "go!". Two similar words, two very different tones.

**वाला — the most productive suffix in Hindi.** It means "the person or thing that deals with …": **ऑटो वाला** (auto driver), **चाय वाला** (tea seller), **दूध वाला** (milkman), **अख़बार वाला** (newspaper man). It also attaches to adjectives and places: **लाल वाला** (the red one), **दिल्ली वाला** (a Delhi person), **आने वाला** (the coming one). It follows gender: वाला · वाली · वाले. ⚠️ Calling someone *भैया* is far more polite than calling them *ऑटो वाला* to their face.

after: ⚠️ Learn the last row exactly as it is. **आप क्या करते हैं?** is a question about your **job**; **आप क्या कर रहे हैं?** is about **this moment**. Mixing them up makes for a funny conversation, and almost every beginner does it once.

grammars.title: Vehicles and places
after: ⚠️ **In India, होटल often means a place to eat**, not to stay. Lodgings are usually called **होटल** too, but a roadside sign saying *होटल* with tables and benches is almost certainly an eatery. If you're looking for a room, ask for a **रहने के लिए होटल**.

sections.title: Getting a ride without getting fleeced

blocks.text: In many Indian cities, auto and taxi fares are negotiated before you set off. It isn't a scam, it's the custom — but as a foreigner you'll be quoted a higher price, and knowing the phrases makes a big difference.

blocks.title: Four things worth knowing
items: **Agree on the price before you get in, not after.** Once you're seated, your bargaining power is gone. Ask *कितना लोगे?* while you're still standing.
**Know roughly what's fair.** Ask your host or the hotel staff before you go out. Once you know the number, stating it calmly is usually enough.
**Ride-hailing apps change everything.** In big cities, apps set fixed fares and most of the haggling disappears. But in small towns and around stations, you'll still need the phrases above.
⚠️ **Don't bargain angrily.** Haggling in India is a relaxed conversation, and people who bargain with a smile almost always get a better price than people who bargain with a tense face.

blocks.text: Rahul's last line — **यही तो दिल्ली है** — is worth keeping. The pattern: **यही** ("this very thing, this is") + **तो** (emphasis) + an ordinary sentence. It's used to accept something as it is, half complaining, half fond: *यही तो ज़िंदगी है* (that's life), *यही तो मुश्किल है* (that's exactly the problem). One short pattern, and once you use it in the right place, you'll sound far more fluent than you really are.
